objects.text: Twelve homes that whisper, not shout
Ceramicist Leila Haddad on slow craft
Why less, done well, is more
Architect Samir Aziz on space and light
Photographed at Villa Serena, Al Barari. Styling by Studio Lune.
“The most beautiful rooms are the ones that are truly lived in.”

There is a particular kind of quiet that settles over a home once it has been edited with care. Nothing shouts; everything has a reason to be there. Over the past year we visited twelve homes across the Gulf and Europe to understand how their owners found that calm, and what they were willing to let go of to get there.

Most of all, they were about rituals. A reading chair placed exactly where the sun lands at four o’clock. A kitchen table long enough for every cousin. A balcony with nothing on it but two chairs and a lemon tree. Small decisions, repeated, become a way of living.

The answers were rarely about money. They were about light — where it falls in the morning, how it softens through linen in the afternoon — and about materials that age gracefully: oak that darkens, brass that warms, limestone that remembers every footstep.

In the pages that follow you will meet the architects, collectors and families behind these spaces, and you will find practical ideas you can borrow — whatever the size of your home or budget.
How twelve families created homes that feel calm, warm and deeply personal — without the clutter.

“Empty space is where the eye rests.”
Where does a project begin for you?
With a long conversation and a cup of tea. I want to understand how a family moves through their day before I draw a single line.
What is one mistake people make?
Filling every corner. Empty space is not wasted space — it is where the eye rests.
Lime plaster. It is breathable, beautiful in low light and kind to the planet.

objects.text: The founders rewriting the region’s rules
Where the smart money is going next
The stack our founders swear by
Cover: Aisha Rahman, founder of Leap Health, photographed in Abu Dhabi.
“Great companies are built in the boring middle, not at the launch party.”

Five years ago most of the founders in this issue were still at university, working night shifts or quietly building side projects after work. Today their companies employ more than four thousand people across the region and serve customers in over thirty countries.

They are also unusually honest about failure. Almost every founder we spoke to had shut down at least one product before finding the one that worked — and each described that moment as the most useful lesson of their career.

What they share is not a single big idea but a habit of shipping small things quickly, listening to customers obsessively and fixing what breaks before anyone notices. Several started with less than AED 20,000 and a borrowed laptop.

Over the next pages you will find their stories, the tools they rely on and the advice they wish someone had given them on day one.
Meet the young founders turning ideas into companies — and the habits that got them there.

“Hire slowly, listen fast, ship every week.”
What made you start Leap Health?
My mother waited four months for a specialist. I knew software could shorten that queue, so I quit my job and built the first version in my kitchen.
Hiring for speed instead of values. We moved fast for six months and then spent a year fixing the culture.
Talk to ten customers every week, forever. The day you stop listening is the day you start losing.
